paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Water is a life-giver as well as a life-taker. It spans the majority of our planet's surface and has had a significant role in human evolution. According to current projections, it is a factor that will become even more important.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Water has played a vital role in our lives throughout history. Water has always had a thorny relationship with humanity, on the one hand providing immense benefits not only as a supply of drinking water, but also as a source of food, a means of transportation, and a means of trade. However, because people have been obliged to live near water in order to survive and thrive, the relationship has not always been pleasant or productive. In fact, it has been quite the opposite. What started out as a survival necessity has turned out to have a highly destructive and life-threatening side in many cases.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: People and their environment have been hit by big floods and long droughts throughout history, making it harder for them to fight for their lives. The dramatic changes in the environment that we hear about in the news every day are not new. Fields that used to be green and full of life are now empty. Lakes and rivers that used to be full of life are now empty. Savannas have become deserts. What might be new is our childlike amazement at the forces of nature.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Today, we know more about how climates change around the world. Floods in faraway places have an immediate effect on the whole world. Maybe these things make us feel better when floods and other natural disasters are destroying our own property.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: In 2002, floods in several parts of Europe caused a lot of damage that cost billions of euros to fix. Properties all over the continent fell into the sea as waves thumped the coast and destroyed sea defences. But it was not just the sea. Rivers that were swollen by heavy rains and the loss of trees carried large amounts of water that ruined many communities.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The costly short-term solution is to build better and more sophisticated flood defences along rivers. There are less complicated options. Tree planting in highland areas, not just in Europe, but also in locations like the Himalayas, to safeguard people living in low-lying areas like the Ganges Delta, is a less expensive and more appealing alternative. Countries are already being persuaded that the release of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases is causing significant environmental damage. In this area, however, further work is needed.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What about the future? According to projections, two-thirds of the world's population would be without fresh water by 2025. However, the future has arrived in a rising number of parts of the planet. While floods have wreaked havoc in certain areas, water scarcity is generating strife in others. The Rio Grande failed to reach the Gulf of Mexico for the first time in 50 years in the spring of 2002, pitting region against region as they compete for water supplies. Due to drought and growing water usage in many regions of the world, there is currently discussion of water becoming the new oil.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Other doom-laden predictions claim that, as the polar ice caps melt, coastal regions and some low-lying islands will almost certainly be drowned by the water. Popular exotic sites, which are today frequented by tens of thousands of tourists, will become no-go zones. Today's vacation attractions in southern Europe and others will literally become hotspots, making them too hot to live in or visit. It's impossible not to despair in light of the current weather's irregular behavior.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: Some may argue that this pessimism is unfounded, but there has been plenty of evidence that something is wrong with the climate. Flooding has been destructive in many regions of the globe. The catastrophe shifts from one continent to the next as the seasons change. The cost in human life is sad, and the environmental impact is worrying. We'll have to get used to it.

paragraphs.text: John Vesty says that the time has come to bring back to Britain the native animals that have vanished. A poem from around 598 AD describes the hunting of a mystery animal called llewyn. What was it? Nothing fitted until 2006, when an animal bone was found in the Kinsey Cave in northern England, dating from around the same period. Until this discovery, the lynx, a large spotted cat with tasselled ears, was assumed to have died out in Britain at least 6,000 years ago, before the inhabitants of these islands took up farming. But the 2006 find, together with others in Yorkshire and Scotland, makes it evident that the lynx and the mysterious llewyn were the same. If so, the estimated extinction date of the tassel-eared cat moves forward by roughly 5,000 years.

However, this is not the last glimpse of the animal in British culture. A 9th-century stone cross from the Isle of Eigg shows, alongside the deer, boar and aurochs pursued by a mounted hunter, a speckled cat with tasselled ears. We cannot be completely sure, because the animal's backside has been damaged over time and the lynx's stubby tail is unmistakable. But even without this feature, it is difficult to see what else the creature could be. Now the lynx has become the totemic animal of a movement that is transforming British environmentalism: rewilding.

Rewilding means the mass restoration of damaged ecosystems. It involves letting trees return to areas that have been stripped of them, allowing parts of the seabed to recover from trawling and dredging, and permitting rivers to flow freely again. Above all, it means bringing back missing species. One of the most important findings of modern ecology is that ecosystems without large predators behave differently from those that retain them. Some of these predators drive dynamic processes that resonate through the whole food chain, creating niches for hundreds of species that might otherwise struggle to survive. The killers turn out to be bringers of life.

These findings present a great challenge to British conservation, which has often selected arbitrary assemblages of plants and animals and sought, at great effort and expense, to prevent them from changing. It has tried to preserve the living world as if it were a jar of pickles, letting nothing in and nothing out, and keeping nature in an arrested state. But ecosystems are not merely collections of species; they also depend on the dynamic and changing relationships between them. And this dynamism often depends on large predators.

At sea, the potential is even greater. If large areas are protected from commercial fishing, we could once again see what 18th-century literature describes: vast shoals of fish chased by fin and sperm whales within sight of the English shore. This policy would also greatly increase catches in the surrounding seas; the fishing industry's insistence on scouring every part of the seabed, leaving no breeding reserves, could not be more damaging to its own interests.

Rewilding is a rare example of an environmental movement in which campaigners articulate what they are for rather than only what they are against. One of the reasons why enthusiasm for rewilding is spreading so quickly in Britain is that it creates a more inspiring vision than the green movement's usual promise of ‘Follow us and the world will be less awful than it would otherwise be.’

The lynx presents no threat to human beings: there is no known instance of a lynx preying on people. It is a specialist predator of roe deer, a species that has exploded in Britain in recent decades, holding back, through intensive browsing, attempts to re-establish forests. It will also winkle out sika deer, an exotic species that is almost impossible for human beings to control, as it hides in impenetrable plantations of young trees. The attempt to reintroduce this predator marries well with the aim of bringing forests back to parts of our bare and barren uplands. The lynx requires deep cover, and so presents little risk to sheep and other livestock, which, as a condition of farm subsidies, are supposed to be kept out of the woods.

On a recent trip to the Cairngorm Mountains, several conservationists suggested that the lynx could be reintroduced there within 20 years. If trees return to the bare hills elsewhere in Britain, the big cats could follow. Seen from the perspective of anywhere else in Europe, there is nothing extraordinary about these proposals. The lynx has now been reintroduced to mountains in the Alps, in eastern France and in Germany, and has re-established itself in many other places. Since 1970, the European population has tripled to nearly 10,000. Like wolves, bears, boar, bison, moose and other species, the lynx has been able to spread as farming has left the hills and people have discovered that it is more profitable to protect wildlife than to hunt it, as tourists will pay to see it. Large-scale rewilding is happening almost everywhere except Britain.

Here, attitudes are beginning to change. Conservationists are starting to accept that the jar-of-pickles model is failing, even on its own terms. Projects such as Trees for Life in the Highlands give a hint of what might be coming. An organisation has been set up that seeks to catalyse the rewilding of land and sea across Britain, and its aim is to reintroduce that rarest of species to British ecosystems: hope.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The sixteenth and seventeenth centuries saw two great pioneers of modern science: Gilbert and Galileo. Their eminent findings made a big impact. Gilbert was the accredited father of the science of electricity and magnetism, the first modern scientist, a physician at the court of Elizabeth and an Englishman of learning. Before him, all that was known about electricity and magnetism was what the ancients knew, and nothing more than that: lodestone had magnetic properties, and amber and jet, when rubbed, would attract bits of paper or other substances of small specific gravity. However, he has not been given the recognition he deserves.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Gilbert was born before Galileo. He was born on 24 May 1544 into an esteemed family in the UK's Colchester county. After going to grammar school, he went to study medicine at St John's College, Cambridge. He graduated in 1573, then travelled on the continent and later settled down in London.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: He was a very eminent and successful doctor and was elected president of the Royal Science Society. He was appointed personal physician to the Queen (Elizabeth I) and was later knighted by her. He served her faithfully until her death. However, he did not outlive the Queen for long: he died on 10 December 1603, only a few months after his appointment as personal physician to King James.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Although Gilbert was first interested in chemistry, he later changed his focus because of the large amount of mysticism involved in alchemy (such as the transmutation of metal). He gradually became interested in physics through the great minds of the ancient world, particularly the knowledge the ancient Greeks had about lodestones, strange minerals with the power to attract iron. Meanwhile, in 1588, when the Spanish Armada was defeated, Britain became a major seafaring nation, paving the way for the British settlement of America. British ships relied on the magnetic compass, yet no one knew why it worked. Was there a magnetic mountain at the pole, as described in the Odyssey, which ships would never approach? Or, as Columbus said, did the Pole Star attract it? From 1580, William Gilbert conducted ingenious experiments to understand magnetism for almost 20 years.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Gilbert's discoveries were very important to modern physics. He investigated the nature of electricity and magnetism, and he was the one who coined the word ‘electric’. Early beliefs about magnetism were mixed with superstitions, such as the idea that rubbing garlic on lodestone can remove its magnetism. Sailors even believed that the smell of garlic would interfere with the action of the compass, which is why helmsmen were forbidden to eat it near a ship's compass. Gilbert also found that metals can be magnetised by rubbing materials such as fur or plastic on them. He named the ends of a magnet the ‘north pole’ and the ‘south pole’. Depending on their polarity, magnets can attract or repel each other; in addition, however, a magnet always attracts ordinary iron. Though he started to study the relationship between electricity and magnetism, he did not finish it. His research on static electricity using jet and amber only showed that objects with electrical charges can work like magnets, attracting small pieces of paper and similar materials. It was a Frenchman, du Fay, who discovered that there are actually two electrical charges, negative and positive.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: He also questioned traditional astronomical beliefs. Though he was a Copernican, he did not express in his quintessential beliefs whether the earth is at the centre of the universe or in orbit around the sun. He believed that stars are not equidistant from the earth and that they have their own earth-like planets orbiting around them. Compasses always point north because the earth is like a giant magnet: the earth's polarity and the axis it spins on are aligned. He likened the polarity of the earth to that of a magnet and built an entire magnetic philosophy on this analogy. He explained that magnetism was the soul of the earth, and that a perfectly spherical lodestone, when aligned with the earth's poles, would keep moving by itself in 24 hours. He further believed that suns and other stars wobble just like the earth does around a crystal core, and theorised that the moon might also be a magnet that orbits because of its attraction towards the earth. This was perhaps the first proposal that a force might cause a heavenly orbit.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: His research methods were revolutionary in that he used experiments instead of the reasoning and pure logic of the ancient Greek philosophers. This was new in scientific investigation, as scientific experiments had not been in fashion until then. Because of this scientific attitude and his contribution to the field of magnetism, the unit of magnetomotive force, also known as magnetic potential, was named Gilbert in his honour. His approach of careful observation and experimentation, rather than reliance on the authoritative opinion or deductive philosophy of others, laid the very foundation for modern science.
